question: Can gradients through Evo2-7B pre-filter positions for exact substitution rescoring?
setup: Seeded pseudo-random ACGT window (the probe accepts no DNA); gradient of summed next-base log-likelihood w.r.t. input embeddings; first-order substitution estimate vs exact rescoring on 96 sampled substitutions.
findings: Evo2.forward hardcodes torch.no_grad; the inner vtx model must be called directly.
Weights are inference tensors; autograd needs them cloned into normal tensors first (extra memory).
Backward completes at 512 and 2,048 bp with finite gradients; the full 8,192 bp window runs out of GPU memory (48 GB peak) without activation checkpointing.
First-order gradient estimates agree weakly with exact rescoring at 512 bp and at chance by 2,048 bp, so they are not a reliable pre-filter on this test.
With activation checkpointing the full 8,192 bp window fits (20.4 GB peak, 7.1 s backward) and the backward-path reference score matches the forward score.

On the real window, gradient estimates agree moderately with exact rescoring (Spearman 0.50, 24 pairs) but underestimate large effects: the HBB variant is estimated at -1.7 against an exact -21.0, though it ranks 84th of 8,192 positions, so the gradient is usable as a coarse pre-filter, not as a score.
limitations: Random DNA has small, noisy effects (median |delta| about 0.25); a real regulatory window may behave differently and was not tested.
96 sampled substitutions per length gives wide intervals; embedding gradients are bf16.
No activation checkpointing or integrated gradients were tried.
